messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
In the quoted lines, Majeed’s earlier cunning and apathy are not shown as open cruelty, but they can still be sensed. The fragment does not give us a tender, consoling speech. It gives us a decision already made: “I am going to take both of you to the village.” The verb “take” is imperative; it treats Rahima and Jamila as two persons to be moved to a destination. Jamila is carried in a “thin quilt,” which is practical rather than emotionally warm. Rahima is “bewildered,” which suggests she is being acted upon, not fully involved in the decision. The “brilliant moonlight” momentarily blinds Majeed, and that may make him seem less calculating in this instant, but it also keeps the scene visually sharp and morally ambiguous. So I do find a faint trace of the same character: not a sudden saint, but a decisive, somewhat detached agent who controls the movement of the others.

On the deontology/teleology question, I would lean toward teleology. If Majeed were acting primarily from deontological good-will, the emphasis would likely be on their welfare as an end in itself: he would check whether they are safe, reassure them, show concern for their dignity, or frame the movement as a duty owed to them. Instead, the line emphasizes a plan and an outcome. He has already decided to take them to the village. The action is goal-directed: remove them from the present place, carry Jamila, bring Rahima along, reach the village. That fits a teleological motive: he is acting because the consequences seem necessary or useful—perhaps to avoid exposure, prevent harm, preserve his own position, or manage a dangerous situation. The protection is real, but the motive can be read as calculated rather than purely altruistic.

Thus, the quoted lines do not make Majeed clearly malicious. They make him ambiguous: a rescuer in effect, but not necessarily a rescuer in pure moral intention. Given his earlier portrayal, the action is more likely a well-calculated protective move than a disinterested moral impulse.

Single-word palindromes: kayak, level, radar, civic, refer, rotor, rotator, repaper, redder, reviver, deified, redivider.
